mcpSurface.whereTheWriteWouldHaveToLand: In THIS product's existing gate, not in the MCP server. The MCP's single seam into this product is `dashboardsFetch<T>()` (src/dashboards-client.ts:35), whose options are `authorization: 'service' | 'omit'` plus an optional `hauskaKey` -- that is, the service Bearer (DASHBOARDS_API_KEY) or the caller's presented Hauska product key forwarded as x-hauska-key (dashboards-tools.ts:114-121: `const hauskaKey = getCurrentAuthContext()?.presented_key`). NO STAFF IDENTITY IS PRESENTED ANYWHERE ON THIS PATH.
mcpSurface.whatThatMeansInProductTerms: caller.kind for an MCP-driven read is 'product' (or anonymous for template-city), so recordStaffRead returns {recorded:false, reason:'not_a_staff_read'} and the read is SERVED AND UNRECORDED -- and it is not refused, correctly, because a product key is not a person looking at a record. So the MCP clause cannot be met by a store on the MCP side without creating a second writer and a second trail.
mcpSurface.whatTheCardHasToAnswer: (1) Identity propagation: the MCP tool call must carry the CALLING PERSON's staff identity (sub + tenant) and forward it to this product as a staff bearer instead of/as well as the product key, so that the product's gate records a person. (2) If the MCP has no staff identity to forward -- its own callers present product keys -- then no MCP read can be attributed to a person, and 'who looked' must say so as a declared absence rather than an empty table. (3) The write itself needs nothing new: this lane's gate already refuses or records every content read, so a staff-bearing MCP read would be recorded with zero further product work. That is the shape of the card: identity at the MCP boundary, writer unchanged.

A refusals-on-read audit trail cannot use an in-memory fallback on a deployed instance: each instance keeps its own, so 'who looked' answers 'nobody' for reads that really happened. K_SERVICE (the deployment-posture signal already used elsewhere) is what distinguishes the two.

The scoping key for an audit row is the READER's tenant, not the pack's. A bastrop_tx person reading the template pack must file under bastrop_tx, or the row shows up under the city that was read and not the one that read.

A refusal status carries a cause and collapsing the causes loses the finding: 'you may not' (403), 'this deployment cannot keep its own audit trail' (503), and 'this product called its own gate wrong' (500) are three different pages, and only the first is the caller's problem.

Count the seams, do not remember them. The no-bypass guard is two assertions over source text (2 packContentReadStatus call sites, 11 checks -> 12 writes) and it caught a deliberately reintroduced inline block on the first try. A structural count is what can see the route nobody remembered.

When a structural count legitimately differs from the naive expectation, derive it from the read reason (one check, two serving paths on /api/domains/:id -> checks+1 writes) and write the reason into the test, rather than relaxing the assertion.

An unverified or expired bearer on a PUBLIC-FREE pack does not produce a refusal: it resolves as anonymous and the pack is served. A test or falsifier that wants to observe a staff refusal must use a tenant-private pack, or it will assert a refusal that never happens.

`process.exit()` in a Node probe on Windows aborts with `!(handle->flags & UV_HANDLE_CLOSING)` (src/win/async.c:76) while the loopback server and fetch handles are closing. Use `process.exitCode` and let the loop drain.
